newsitem.title: USA: Clinton admin. denies politicizing citizenship.
newsitem.headline: Clinton admin. denies politicizing citizenship.

text.p: The Clinton administration Wednesday said there was no truth to allegations that citizenship applications were sped up this year in hopes of adding more Democrats to the voter rolls this November.
The Immigration and Naturalisation Service estimated a record 1.1 million new American citizens were sworn in around the country in the year ending Sept. 30, 1996, more than double the previous year.

"The naturalisation process cannot and should not be politicized," INS executive associate commissioner T. Alexander Aleinikoff testified at a hearing of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration.

He said the agency maintained the same standards for these recent applicants as it had for others. "We did not lower the standards," he said, adding that the higher numbers were due to hiring of more employees to handle what he termed "a sea of applications."

The Republican chairman of the panel, retiring Sen. Alan Simpson, said he was concerned there might have been political motivation behind the decision to add INS employees and take other steps to help immigrants become American voters.
"I am concerned that partisan desires may have pushed the INS more swiftly than is desirable," Simpson of Wyoming said.

Democratic Sen. Edward Kennedy of Massachusetts called it "poetic justice" that many immigrants were rushing to become citizens this year in reaction to the anti-immigrant legislation pushed by Republican congressional leaders.

He said the agency should be praised for making much needed improvements in the way it handled a backlog of citizenship applications. "Yet we now hear complaints from some Republicans that INS is doing its job too well, and that it is doing so for partisan political reasons. Nonsense."

The INS received 300,000 applications for citizenship in 1992. By 1995 the number had tripled and processing was backed up two years before INS Commissioner Doris Meissner received congressional support to speed up the applications by hiring more personnel. The waiting time for processing is now back to the usual six months.
